headline: GYG exits US market, booking $26.7 million net loss, with founder Steven Marks conceding the Chicago expansion took too long to reach required scale.
reasoning: Marks reflected that while the food quality and guest experience in Chicago were strong, it took too long to build the right team and the timeline to reach necessary scale was unacceptable for a public company. He acknowledged he would have done things differently but concluded the decision to exit was correct from a capital management perspective. The US exit resulted in a $26.7 million net loss for the year, though underlying earnings from continuing operations remained strong.
quote: I would have been in Chicago right now and I think, you know, being over there with their team for three plus months, you know, but there's a lot you learn, right. And there's a lot of mistakes that you make. And you know and I would have done a lot of things differently. But but I'll tell you it's I mean the food was outstanding. So was the guest experience. Took a while to get our teams right and find the people. And I think once I got the team right, it was going to take too long to get to where we had to get to. And, you know, I believed in it. You know, we're a public company. You know, we have to, you know, manage our capital correctly. And it was the right decision to make.
episode_title: GYG hungry for growth after US retreat

headline: GYG managing input and wage cost pressures through revenue-led model and supply chain optimisation
reasoning: Steven Marks acknowledged the broad pressures facing the restaurant industry including rising wages and input costs, but argued GYG is well-positioned through its supply chain discipline led by Dave Hanson. He described GYG as 'revenue junkies', arguing that strong top-line growth driven by great guest experience and appropriate pricing is the key lever to absorb cost inflation. He noted that wage increases of around 5% per year are a known, recurring cost that must be built into the business model rather than treated as a surprise. The strong comp sales growth is what allows franchisee economics to improve despite rising costs.
quote: Well, I mean, the restaurant business, the restaurant business. Right. And the good thing is, man, we understand this business inside and out are cost of goods. You know, led by Dave Hanson, who runs Supply Chain, has never been in better shape, never been in better shape. And that's why we always tell people that we're revenue junkies. Meaning, to build an amazing business, you need amazing revenue. And that's all we care about. And to us, building incredible revenue means you got the guest experience, right? Is your food right? Is it? Is it priced at the right angle? Are you delivering an experience that's better than anybody else? And we keep doing that because, you know, people ask you know, wages, you know, go up 5% a year. That hasn't changed. That's like every year. So you got to factor that into your business.
episode_title: GYG hungry for growth after US retreat

headline: GYG founder Steven Marks bullish on Australian rollout after US exit, flagging 7-800 more restaurants to build and accelerating store openings to 40 per year.
reasoning: Steven Marks acknowledged the US retreat was the right capital management decision, noting the team was not progressing fast enough to justify continued investment. He emphasised the Australian pipeline has never been stronger, with 117 board-approved restaurants in the pipeline, 32 openings in FY26, 35 planned for FY27, and a medium-term target of 40 per year with 85% being drive-throughs. He also highlighted strong underlying earnings growth of 30% year-on-year, record EBITDA of $85 million, and strengthening transaction comps as evidence that customers are visiting more frequently. Growth in Singapore and Japan adds further optionality. He described GYG as a generational business with significant remaining upside.
quote: No. So our pipeline, which are basically board approved commercially agreed terms, has never been strong. We have 117 restaurants. And as you can see today, you know, with our release. Well, we did 32 restaurants this year. You know, 85% of what we're signing off for, drive thrus, which is a big part of our business. We did 32 this year. We'll do 35 next year, and in the medium term, that will start rolling out to 40 restaurants a year. 85% being drive through. So the pipeline has never been stronger. You know, the economics of our restaurants have never been stronger.
episode_title: GYG hungry for growth after US retreat
